label: fiction
title: The Open Door
setting: The court sits in the present-day fictional city of Elloryn. The board of a housing charity met at Carrow House to vote on closing three night shelters. Facilities supervisor Nela Tor asked finance director Oren Vaal to wait in a records room after an anonymous warning predicted violence if he entered the public corridor. The room's door had no lock and remained physically openable. A red fire card outside read, 'NO EXIT UNTIL THE BOARD VOTES.' Oren initially agreed to wait, then asked to leave. The dispute is whether Nela protected him or detained him to control the vote.
elements: The accused intentionally detained or helped to detain an adult against that person’s will.
The accused intended to compel another person or an institution to act as a condition of the hostage’s release.
The accused knew that the detention and demand were unlawful.
hook: The records-room door is unlocked. Oren Vaal still says he cannot leave: Nela Tor stands in the doorway, holds his phone, and tells the board he stays until it votes. The jury must decide when protection became captivity.

accused.human: Nela Tor, 39, supervised maintenance and overnight safety at Carrow House for seven years. She had slept in one of the charity's shelters as a young adult and later trained volunteers in de-escalation. She lived above a bakery with her partner and cared for an elderly neighbour's garden each weekend.
accused.if_guilty: If convicted, the judge would decide sentence later. The jury must assess Nela's intention and knowledge from the evidence, without treating her history with the shelters as either proof of guilt or a moral excuse.

prosecution.speaker: pc
prosecution.text: An unlocked door can still hold a person when someone blocks it, takes the person's phone, and threatens exposure to danger outside. Oren first agreed to wait because Nela showed him an anonymous warning. Ten minutes later he withdrew that agreement. Nela stood across the doorway, kept his phone, placed a red card saying no exit until the board votes, and sent the board a demand: restore all three shelters or Oren remains. Those are deliberate detention, institutional coercion, and knowledge of wrongdoing.

defence.speaker: dc
defence.text: Nela received a frightening warning naming Oren and the public corridor. She moved him to a quiet room, left the door unlocked, and asked the board to resolve the safety risk before he emerged. Oren voluntarily entered and initially thanked her. The red card was crude emergency shorthand, not a lock. Nela's message sought a vote before movement, but she believed that sequence protected Oren from a threatened crowd. The prosecution must exclude an overprotective safety response, not merely prove that Nela handled it badly.

prosecution.speaker: pc
prosecution.text: The lawful purpose ended when Oren said, 'I am leaving now.' Nela answered, 'Not until they reverse it,' took his phone when he tried to call the chair, and put her body across the only doorway. Her board message did not ask for security assistance; it named the price of release. The anonymous warning may explain why Oren entered. It does not justify using his fear as leverage after he withdrew consent. The open latch changes the method, not the reality or intention of detention.

defence.speaker: dc
defence.text: Oren never touched the handle, asked Nela to move, or attempted to pass. He believed the anonymous threat might be real and remained seated while the corridor filled with shouting visitors. Nela held his phone after it displayed a caller's location, which she says risked exposure, and returned it within minutes. Her message linked movement to a vote because the warning itself linked unrest to that vote. The words were reckless and controlling, but they remain consistent with misguided protection rather than hostage-taking beyond reasonable doubt.

epilogue: Carrow House adopted an emergency protocol requiring two trained decision-makers, direct contact with public safety services, and a written record whenever someone was asked to shelter in place. Oren took extended leave and later worked with residents affected by the shelter closures. Volunteers kept a temporary night service open while the board reconsidered funding. Nela's maintenance team was given independent supervision, and staff training began using the difficult distinction between requesting safety and removing another adult's choice.

beats.speaker: pc
beats.text: The parties agree that the board meeting began at 18:00 and that its final item was a proposal to close three night shelters. Oren prepared the financial paper supporting closure; Nela had publicly opposed it at staff meetings. At 18:14, an anonymous message reached Nela's work device: 'Keep the numbers man out of the corridor until the shelter vote ends, or his family learns what a crowd can do.' The author has not been identified. Nela showed the message to Oren and led him into the nearby records room at 18:17.
beats.reveal_note: The warning supplies a genuine protective context and explains Oren's initial consent, but its anonymous author and factual truth remain unproved.

beats.speaker: judge
beats.text: The anonymous warning is admitted only to help you assess Nela's state of mind, Oren's initial decision to enter the room, and the reasonableness of the later protection explanation. It is not admitted as proof that a crowd intended violence, that Oren's family was actually in danger, or that any unidentified person joined Nela in an offence. You must not assume the warning was true merely because it was received. You may consider what Nela did after receiving it, including whether her response changed once Oren withdrew consent and help was offered.
beats.reveal_note: The limited-purpose direction allows the warning to explain belief and initial consent without turning an anonymous allegation into proof of an external danger.

beats.speaker: judge
beats.text: Detention does not require a locked door, physical injury, or a successful attempt to escape. An adult is detained against their will if, in the circumstances, the accused intentionally removes a realistic freedom to leave through force, threat, intimidation, obstruction, or another coercive act. Initial consent can later be withdrawn. On the other hand, a request to remain for safety, even a firm or poorly expressed request, is not detention if the person retains a practical and understood choice to go. Assess Oren's words and conduct, Nela's position and control of the phone, the open door, the warning, and the surrounding corridor.
beats.reveal_note: This focused instruction prevents the unlocked door from deciding the case while preserving the distinction between coercion and a consensual safety request.

beats.speaker: judge
beats.text: The prosecution must prove beyond reasonable doubt that Nela intentionally detained Oren against his will, intended to compel the board to act as a condition of his release, and knew the detention and demand were unlawful. Protection may explain conduct, but it does not authorise one adult to remove another's choice or use that person to secure a vote. Consider when consent changed, whether Oren had a realistic freedom to leave, what Nela's exact messages required, why she held the phone, why she rejected volunteers, and the warning only for its permitted state-of-mind purpose. Nela need not prove that the warning was genuine or identify its sender. If misguided protection remains a reasonable explanation for any charged intention or knowledge, return Not Guilty. Do not research the people or issues online.
beats.reveal_note: The final direction connects consent, practical restraint, conditional compulsion, knowledge of unlawfulness, the limited-purpose warning, and the unchanged burden.

twist: The editorial reference is Guilty because Nela continued after Oren clearly withdrew consent, blocked the only doorway, took his phone, wrote an explicit no-exit card, conditioned his movement on restoring all shelters, and rejected offered safety volunteers. The anonymous warning is relevant only to Nela's state of mind and Oren's initial consent, not proof of an actual crowd threat. The strongest reasonable opposing interpretation remains humane and substantial: the door was unlocked, Oren never attempted to pass, corridor unrest was real, Nela returned the phone within minutes, and each act can be described as an overreaching effort to protect him.

jurors.label: Fen
jurors.persona: Responds first to the image of an open door, then tests whether fear and obstruction removed practical choice.

agree: An unlocked door looks like freedom. That was my first reaction.
pushback: Would Oren reasonably feel free with Nela blocking the doorway and holding his phone?
concede: His calm does not mean consent after he clearly said he was leaving.
burden_drift: I want Nela to prove that Oren could simply have walked past.
burden_correct: The prosecution must prove practical detention; Nela need not demonstrate an escape route.
holdout: I need more than an uncomfortable conversation in a room with no lock.
final: The express refusal, bodily block, and confiscated phone made the open latch meaningless in practice.

jurors.label: Asha
jurors.persona: Distinguishes Oren's initial agreement from his later withdrawal without rewriting either period.

agree: Oren consented at 18:17, so the first ten minutes were not detention.
pushback: At 18:27 he withdrew consent. What lawful basis remained after that point?
concede: The offence can begin after a lawful start; the chronology does not have to be all one thing.
burden_drift: Nela's change of purpose feels obvious once the messages arrive.
burden_correct: We still infer purpose beyond reasonable doubt from the later words and conduct.
holdout: I am dividing the event at the exact point consent changed.
final: After 18:27, every act served the vote condition rather than a consensual shelter request.

jurors.label: Rel
jurors.persona: Insists that the anonymous warning remain within its narrow evidentiary purpose.

agree: The warning can explain belief and consent; it cannot prove an actual threat outside.
pushback: Are we treating anonymous words as true because they make Nela's account easier to understand?
concede: Even accepting Nela's fear, rejecting neutral volunteers and demanding a vote point to a new purpose.
burden_drift: The mystery sender makes me want Nela to solve the origin before I judge her response.
burden_correct: She need not identify the sender; the prosecution must prove what Nela intended and knew.
holdout: I will not convert limited-purpose evidence into proof of danger or conspiracy.
final: Nela's own admitted acts prove the offence without assuming that the anonymous warning was true.

jurors.label: Gavi
jurors.persona: Looks for practical restraint rather than requiring a lock, weapon, or injury.

agree: No lock, no weapon, no injury. Those absences matter.
pushback: A person can still be trapped by a body in the doorway and fear about family.
concede: Taking the phone removed the obvious safe way for Oren to challenge Nela's control.
burden_drift: The red card is so blunt that I may let its slogan replace the full context.
burden_correct: We assess the card with conduct, not as a magic label for guilt.
holdout: Show me how the method actually removed a realistic choice to leave.
final: The combined obstruction, fear, and phone control created practical detention despite the open lock.

jurors.label: Neris · foreperson
jurors.persona: Maps consent, detention, demand, and knowledge as separate issues for the room.

agree: Let's answer four questions: when consent ended, what restrained Oren, what the board was asked to do, and what Nela knew.
pushback: Does protection explain keeping him safe, or using his movement as the price of a vote?
concede: The board message states the exchange directly, and the rejected volunteers undercut necessity.
burden_drift: Nela's poor wording can make us demand a better innocent explanation from her.
burden_correct: Bad wording is evidence only to the extent the prosecution proves its intended meaning.
holdout: I want each element supported without treating the title of the charge as an answer.
final: The later acts prove detention, the messages prove compulsion, and the admissions prove knowledge.

jurors.label: Tomal
jurors.persona: Takes emergency safety work seriously and asks when urgency became domination.

agree: Nela had a real duty to respond to a warning and visible unrest.
pushback: Why reject trained help if the purpose was simply safe movement?
concede: Refusing volunteers until after the vote makes the political condition look deliberate.
burden_drift: A flawed emergency response can look criminal just because a better protocol existed.
burden_correct: The issue is Nela's proved intention, not whether she followed best practice.
holdout: I need the prosecution to mark the point where protection changed purpose.
final: That point is the refusal of help combined with the explicit shelter-vote condition.

jurors.label: Lera
jurors.persona: Changes position when Nela's response to offered help reveals a coercive choice.

agree: At first I see frightened people making imperfect safety decisions.
pushback: If safety was the aim, why refuse two volunteers and insist on the vote first?
concede: That decision turns an emergency explanation into leverage over the board.
burden_drift: Once I move, I could wrongly treat Oren's initial consent as meaningless.
burden_correct: The lawful beginning remains real; guilt depends on what Nela chose later.
holdout: I will change only if the later sequence has a distinct coercive purpose.
final: I have changed because Nela rejected the safe alternative and preserved the voting condition.

jurors.label: Bex
jurors.persona: Tests Oren's account without mistaking a calm response for willing participation.

agree: Oren did not shout, fight, or test the handle.
pushback: People can comply because they are afraid; calm behaviour is not automatic consent.
concede: His exact statement that he was leaving is clearer than any guess from his posture.
burden_drift: I might ask Oren to prove resistance instead of asking whether Nela imposed restraint.
burden_correct: There is no legal requirement that an alleged hostage risk a confrontation or failed escape.
holdout: I want to know what Oren communicated, not what courage we imagine he should show.
final: His withdrawal was unambiguous, and Nela's response confirms she understood and refused it.

jurors.label: Coren
jurors.persona: Identifies with the shelter stakes but refuses to let a worthwhile cause justify coercion.

agree: Closing night shelters would hurt people, and Nela knew that personally.
pushback: A humane cause cannot answer whether she used Oren as leverage.
concede: Her message demanded the exact outcome she wanted as the condition for movement.
burden_drift: Because I oppose the closures too, I could excuse conduct I would condemn for another cause.
burden_correct: Sympathy for the goal is irrelevant to whether the prosecution proves the offence.
holdout: I am putting the shelter policy aside and deciding the treatment of Oren.
final: The good Nela hoped to achieve does not erase the intentional detention she chose.

jurors.label: Vira
jurors.persona: Examines Nela's subjective belief while recognising that belief can change during an event.

agree: The warning gave Nela a credible reason to begin with protection in mind.
pushback: What does her rejection of assistance tell us about her later belief and purpose?
concede: By tying release to the preferred vote, she demonstrated knowledge that she was imposing a condition.
burden_drift: Her experience with shelters makes motive feel clearer than legal knowledge.
burden_correct: We infer knowledge from her words and choices, not from biography.
holdout: I require proof that misguided care became knowing unlawful control.
final: Her own admissions and refusal of a safe alternative establish that transition beyond reasonable doubt.

jurors.label: Pell
jurors.persona: Asks whether the board message is a safety sequence or an exchange imposed on the institution.

agree: Waiting until a corridor settles can be a sensible safety sequence.
pushback: Restoring all three shelters is not a safety measurement; it is the board outcome Nela wanted.
concede: The words 'he walks out' make Oren's movement the price attached to that outcome.
burden_drift: The message is so direct that I may ignore Nela's genuine fear.
burden_correct: We can acknowledge fear and still ask whether the prosecution proved a coercive choice.
holdout: I am reading every part of the message, including the corridor condition that helps the defence.
final: Taken whole and with the rejected volunteers, the message is an exchange rather than a safety update.
